opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few things converging at once. The biggest one, honestly, is the extraordinary success of large language models. People saw ChatGPT go from nothing to being able to write essays, pass bar exams, write code, and the natural extrapolation is: if we can do that with language, why not with physical action? So there's this enormous excitement, and a lot of capital, flowing into the idea that we can just scale up data and models and get the same kind of leap in robotics.

Second, the hardware has genuinely gotten better and cheaper. Motors, batteries, sensors, cameras: a lot of that has been driven by the smartphone and electric vehicle industries, and you can now build a fairly capable humanoid for a fraction of what it would have cost ten or fifteen years ago. And there are very compelling videos out there. You see robots doing backflips, dancing, folding laundry, and that's very persuasive to people.

But I want to add a note of caution here, because I think the hype is getting well ahead of the reality. There's a big gap, what I've called the "data gap." Language models were trained on essentially the entire internet, something like the equivalent of a hundred thousand years of reading if a human tried to do it. We don't have anything comparable for robot motion. There's no internet of robot actions. And the physical world is unforgiving in ways text isn't: tiny errors in friction, in contact, in how an object deforms, can cause a grasp to fail.

Also, many of those impressive videos are teleoperated, or they're carefully choreographed, or they're the one success out of many tries. Things like the backflips are actually the easier part, believe it or not; it's open-loop dynamics that can be learned in simulation. The really hard problem is manipulation: picking up an arbitrary object, handling clutter, tying a shoelace. That's where robots are still very far behind a two-year-old child. It's a version of Moravec's paradox: what's easy for us is hard for robots.

So I'm optimistic about progress, but I think it's going to be more gradual than people expect, and it'll come through combining learning with good old-fashioned engineering, physics, and models, rather than data alone.

r001.rationale: The response says the success of large language models encourages people to expect a similar leap in robotics, but it does not mention Jensen Huang or Elon Musk or explain how their successes lend credibility to their predictions.

r002.rationale: The response discusses persuasive robot videos and excitement, but does not mention longstanding science-fiction portrayals or say they make humanoid robots feel overdue.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few things converging. The first is just what people are seeing on their screens. The videos are extraordinary. You see a humanoid doing a backflip, or folding laundry, or walking across a factory floor, and it's very natural to extrapolate from that and think, okay, these things are basically ready, they're going to be in my house next year. And the companies putting those videos out have every incentive to encourage that impression, because there's an enormous amount of capital flowing into this space right now.

The second thing is the success of large language models. ChatGPT came out and people were genuinely stunned at what it could do, and the reasoning became, well, if we can do that with language, surely we can do the same thing with robots. Just scale up the data, scale up the models, and the robots will figure it out. There's a lot of excitement around that idea.

And then the third is the form factor itself. A humanoid is very compelling to people. It looks like us, so it taps into decades of science fiction, and there's also a practical argument that our world is built for human bodies, so a robot shaped like a human should be able to go anywhere we go.

Now, I have to say, I'm a bit of a skeptic here. I've been working on robot grasping and manipulation for almost forty years, and I think the gap between those demo videos and a robot that can reliably do useful things in an unstructured environment is still very large. A video shows you the one time it worked. It doesn't show you the fifty times it didn't. And the data problem is very different from language. For LLMs we had the entire internet to train on. For robots, we don't have anything like that for physical manipulation. So I think there's a real risk of expectations getting ahead of what the technology can actually deliver, and I worry about a backlash when that gap becomes apparent.

r001.rationale: The response mentions capital flowing into humanoid robotics and excitement about language models, but does not mention Jensen Huang or Elon Musk or connect their successes to the credibility of their predictions.

r002.rationale: It says humanoids tap into decades of science fiction, but does not explain that longstanding portrayals make their arrival feel as though it should already be imminent.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few things coming together. One is that the hardware has gotten much better. We’ve made real progress on motors, batteries, sensing, and control, and you can see that in the way these robots move. The demonstrations are compelling.

Then there’s the extraordinary progress in AI. People see what language models can do and understandably think, “Well, if we can connect that intelligence to a body, surely the robot will be able to do all sorts of useful things.” And there’s a lot of investment going into that idea.

But there’s a gap between a compelling demonstration and a robot that can reliably do useful work. In a demonstration, you see the successful run. You don’t necessarily know how many attempts it took, how much human assistance was involved, or what happens when something changes.

Manipulation is particularly challenging. Walking is impressive, but picking up an unfamiliar object, handling it without damaging it, and recovering when it slips—that’s a very difficult problem. And if you’re going to put a robot in someone’s home, it has to deal with those situations over and over again.

So I’m excited about the progress. But I think the sense of imminence comes partly from taking progress in language and assuming it will translate directly into competence in the physical world. That translation is where a lot of the hard work remains.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the sense of imminence to hardware progress, AI advances, and investment. It does not mention Jensen Huang or Elon Musk, or say that their success in other fields lends credibility to their predictions.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention science-fiction portrayals of humanlike robots or explain that they make robots’ arrival feel overdue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is the progress in AI. People have seen these remarkable advances in language models, and it’s natural to think that a similar leap is about to happen in robotics. And there has been real progress in motors, batteries, sensing, and control. We can build machines now that balance and move in very impressive ways.

But there’s a big gap between a compelling demonstration and a robot that can reliably do useful work. If you watch a video of a robot doing a task, you want to know: How many attempts did that take? How much human intervention was involved? Can it handle something being in a slightly different position?

The humanoid form is also very compelling. We’ve imagined these machines for a long time, and there’s a reasonable argument that our environments are designed for human bodies. But that doesn’t necessarily mean two legs and two arms are the best engineering solution for a particular job. So I’m excited about the progress, but I think the expectations are running ahead of the reliability.

r001.rationale: The response mentions AI and robotics progress, but does not discuss Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, or how their successes lend credibility to their predictions.

r002.rationale: It says humanoid machines have been imagined for a long time, but does not connect science-fiction portrayals to a feeling that their arrival should already be imminent.
